source.title: Cardiovascular Implications of the Enhanced Games: Performance Enhancing Drugs in Competition and Recreation

paper.citation: Vecchiato M., Palermi S., Zamodics M., Babity M., Eftekhari M., Ryali R., et al. Cardiovascular Implications of the Enhanced Games: Performance Enhancing Drugs in Competition and Recreation. Sports Medicine - Open. 2026;12(1):48. doi:10.1186/s40798-026-01026-9.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What ergogenic and cardiovascular evidence exists for PED classes relevant to pharmacologically enhanced sport, and what screening and monitoring framework is justified? Participants: No new cohort; the review synthesizes studies of PED-exposed athletes and nonathletes. Sport and level: Enhanced Games, elite/recreational strength athletes, and the broader recreational-use context. Design: Narrative clinical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: AAS, growth hormone/IGF-1, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, stimulants, β2-agonists, diuretics, metabolic modulators, and incretin-based weight-management therapies.
paper.tldr: Across drug classes, ergogenic evidence was inconsistent; the review judged AAS and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to have the clearest performance signals alongside associations with myocardial remodeling, arrhythmia, and thrombotic events. Much existing evidence consisted of case reports, small series, scarce registries, nonathlete data, and cohorts confounded by comorbidity and polypharmacy/“stacking.” When PED exposure is disclosed, use a nonjudgmental harm-reduction pathway with sports-medicine/cardiology oversight, exact exposure history, baseline evaluation, and longitudinal follow-up.
paper.methods: Design: Narrative clinical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: AAS, growth hormone/IGF-1, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, stimulants, β2-agonists, diuretics, metabolic modulators, and incretin-based weight-management therapies. Comparator: PED-exposed versus nonexposed evidence where available; otherwise mechanistic, case, small-cohort, or clinical-population evidence. Measurements and outcomes: Ergogenic effects, cardiac structure/function, blood pressure, rhythm, thrombotic events, metabolic effects, and screening markers. Analysis: Narrative synthesis with proposed risk-adapted preparticipation and longitudinal monitoring; no pooled quantitative analysis.
paper.findings: Across drug classes, ergogenic evidence was inconsistent; the review judged AAS and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to have the clearest performance signals alongside associations with myocardial remodeling, arrhythmia, and thrombotic events. Much existing evidence consisted of case reports, small series, scarce registries, nonathlete data, and cohorts confounded by comorbidity and polypharmacy/“stacking.” Exposure characterization was often inadequate for compound, cumulative dose, duration, and use pattern, so much evidence supports association rather than causation and cannot precisely quantify cardiovascular risk. The authors propose individualized baseline cardiovascular screening plus serial reassessment and, when indicated, advanced imaging and rhythm monitoring; they state no dedicated evidence-based eligibility thresholds exist for enhanced athletes.
paper.limitations: This narrative review did not report a reproducible systematic search, risk-of-bias assessment, or pooled effects. Evidence underrepresented women, non-White athletes, elite competitors, and well-characterized doses; selection and publication bias were plausible. Medical oversight in an observational enhanced-sport setting cannot remove confounding or establish safety, and the authors explicitly reject treating the Enhanced Games as proof of safe enhancement. Additional transfer limitation — interpretation: This review supports referral and surveillance, not institutional approval of PED use or a dosing protocol.
paper.practicalImplications: When PED exposure is disclosed, use a nonjudgmental harm-reduction pathway with sports-medicine/cardiology oversight, exact exposure history, baseline evaluation, and longitudinal follow-up. Do not imply that medical supervision makes supraphysiologic use safe; the evidence is heterogeneous, causal dose–response data are sparse, and standard athlete-heart findings may overlap with early toxicity.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, when PED exposure is disclosed, use a nonjudgmental harm-reduction pathway with sports-medicine/cardiology oversight, exact exposure history, baseline evaluation, and longitudinal follow-up. Do not imply that medical supervision makes supraphysiologic use safe; the evidence is heterogeneous, causal dose–response data are sparse, and standard athlete-heart findings may overlap with early toxicity. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
